prompt.context: Your client is an entrepreneur looking to invest in a new sports bar. He needs to determine how profitable the business will be and convince his primary investor — his father — that it will be a viable business.
prompt.question: What factors would you consider and investigate to assess the profitability of the sports bar, and ultimately, should the father invest?

clarifying_info.q: What does the average customer spend on food per visit?
What does the average customer spend on drinks per visit?

clarifying_info.a: Food costs are 80% of food revenues
Drinks costs are 50% of drinks revenues

clarifying_info.q: What are the labor costs and staffing needs?
clarifying_info.a: Kitchen: 4 people at $10/hour (open hours only); Bar: 1 person at $5/hour; Waitresses: 3 people at $5/hour

clarifying_info.q: How many customers come in per hour?
clarifying_info.a: Sunday–Wednesday day (12–8pm): 10 food customers/hour, 4 drinks customers/hour; Sunday–Wednesday night (8pm–12am): 4 food/hour, 15 drinks/hour. Thursday–Saturday day (12–8pm): 15 food/hour, 5 drinks/hour; Thursday–Saturday night (8pm–2am): 5 food/hour, 20 drinks/hour
The client estimates $500K in start-up capital (renovations, equipment, licenses)

clarifying_info.q: Are there other costs such as utilities, insurance, or marketing?
clarifying_info.a: There is no specific data on utilities, legal, insurance, licenses, training, remodeling, equipment, and other startup costs beyond the $500K figure

framework: Revenues: estimate weekly food and drink revenues based on customer volume, hours, and average spend
COGS: apply food (80%) and drinks (50%) cost percentages to weekly revenues
Labor costs: calculate weekly hours for kitchen, bar, and waitstaff across all operating days and shifts
Fixed costs: convert monthly lease ($10K) to weekly cost
Weekly and annual profit: aggregate all revenue and cost lines
Break-even and ROI: compare annual profit against $500K start-up investment; compute payback period and 5-year ROI
Recommendation: frame profitability vs. alternative investment opportunities; identify risks and ways to improve margins

questions.prompt: Calculate total weekly food and drink orders, then weekly revenue
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a structured table. Sun–Wed (4 days): day shift (8 hrs) food=10/hr → 80 food orders/day; drinks=4/hr → 32 drinks/day. Night shift (4 hrs) food=4/hr → 16 food/day; drinks=15/hr → 60 drinks/day. Daily totals: 96 food, 92 drinks. Weekly (×4 days): 384 food, 368 drinks. Thu–Sat (3 days): day shift (8 hrs) food=15/hr → 120 food/day; drinks=5/hr → 40 drinks/day. Night shift (6 hrs) food=5/hr → 30 food/day; drinks=20/hr → 120 drinks/day. Daily totals: 150 food, 160 drinks. Weekly (×3 days): 450 food, 480 drinks. Total weekly food orders = 834; total weekly drink orders = 848. Revenue: food = 834×$15 = $12,510; drinks = 848×$20 = $16,960; total weekly revenue = $29,470.

math.setup: Weekly orders by shift × price per order
steps: Sun–Wed day: food 10×8=80, drinks 4×8=32 per day
Sun–Wed night: food 4×4=16, drinks 15×4=60 per day
Thu–Sat day: food 15×8=120, drinks 5×8=40 per day
Thu–Sat night: food 5×6=30, drinks 20×6=120 per day

questions.guidance: Apply the given percentages to each revenue stream. Food COGS = 80% of $12,510 = $10,008. Drinks COGS = 50% of $16,960 = $8,480. Total weekly COGS = $19,488.

math.setup: COGS = cost % × weekly revenue by category

questions.guidance: Calculate total hours per week for each staff group, then multiply by pay rate. Kitchen (open all hours): Sun–Wed 4 days × 12 hrs (12pm–12am) = 48 hrs; Thu–Sat 3 days × 14 hrs (12pm–2am) = 42 hrs; total kitchen hours = 90. Bar and Waitresses same schedule: 48+42=90 hrs each. Kitchen: 4 people × $10 × 90 hrs = $3,600. Bar: 1 person × $5 × 90 hrs = $450. Waitresses: 3 people × $5 × 90 hrs = $1,350. Total weekly labor = $5,400.

math.setup: Total weekly hours per role × pay rate × number of staff
steps: Kitchen hours: Sun–Wed 4×12=48 hrs + Thu–Sat 3×14=42 hrs = 90 hrs
Bar hours: same schedule = 90 hrs; 1 person × $5/hr × 90 hrs = $450
Waitress hours: same = 90 hrs; 3 people × $5/hr × 90 hrs = $1,350

questions.prompt: Calculate weekly profit and annual profit
questions.guidance: Lease is $10,000/month; assume 4 weeks/month → $2,500/week. Weekly profit = revenue − COGS − labor − lease = $29,470 − $19,488 − $5,400 − $2,500 = $2,082. Annual profit (assume 50 operating weeks) = $2,082 × 50 = $104,100. Note that other costs (utilities, marketing, insurance) are excluded and would reduce actual profit.

math.setup: Weekly profit = revenue − COGS − labor − weekly lease; Annual = weekly profit × 50 weeks

questions.prompt: Calculate break-even period and 5-year ROI on the $500K start-up investment
questions.guidance: Break-even = $500,000 / $104,100 ≈ 4.8 years. 5-year ROI = ((annual profit × 5) − start-up cost) / start-up cost = ($520,500 − $500,000) / $500,000 = 4.1%. The father should compare this against other investment opportunities; the ROI is less than 1% per year, which is very low.

math.setup: Break-even = up-front costs / annual profit; 5-yr ROI = (5-yr cumulative profit − investment) / investment

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and additional considerations should the father weigh before investing?

categories.name: Excluded costs
ideas: Insurance and legal fees not included
Licenses and training costs not included

categories.name: Revenue risks
ideas: Sudden rise in COGS due to food shortages or supply disruption
Decrease in customer traffic after initial novelty wears off

categories.name: Cost risks
ideas: Increase in minimum wage raising labor costs
Equipment breakdown requiring unplanned capital expenditure

categories.name: Strategic improvements
ideas: Add revenue streams: jukebox, advertising, private event bookings
Optimize food vs. drinks mix to shift toward higher-margin drinks
Reduce start-up costs by purchasing used equipment or a simpler interior redesign
Build brand loyalty to justify higher prices over time
Consider location carefully relative to sports-fan density and competitor presence

recommendation: The sports bar is projected to be profitable on an operating basis (~$104K/year), but the 4.8-year payback period and ~4.1% cumulative 5-year ROI are very low relative to the $500K investment required
The father could likely find alternative investments with a faster payback and higher annual return; the bar does not clear a compelling investment hurdle on financials alone

If the client is strategically motivated (e.g., lifestyle, brand-building), he should at minimum close the cost gap by reducing start-up expenditures and identifying additional revenue streams before seeking commitment from his father
risks: Several cost categories (utilities, marketing, insurance) were excluded and will reduce actual profitability
Revenue is sensitive to customer traffic assumptions; a modest decline in foot traffic could eliminate the thin margin
Rising minimum wages or food supply shocks could quickly turn the business unprofitable
next_steps: Conduct a full cost model including all excluded line items to refine the profit estimate
Benchmark ROI against comparable small-business investments or index funds
Explore start-up cost reductions (used equipment, phased renovation) to shorten break-even
Identify incremental revenue opportunities (jukebox, events, advertising) before finalizing the business plan
